question: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Liquefy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is LIQUEFY, meaning to make or become liquid.

 

• The difficulty is that the vowel before -fy is an E, although the related word *liquid* has an i. The word comes from Latin liquefacere, and the e belongs to the *-facere* half.

 

• Only four common English verbs end in -EFY; every other verb of this kind ends in -IFY:

 

• LIQUEFY, PUTREFY, RAREFY, STUPEFY

 

• Against them stand *classify, justify, magnify, notify, purify, satisfy, testify* — and dozens more, all -ify.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The related noun is liquefaction, which keeps the e — as in *liquefied petroleum gas (LPG)*.

 

• The other three exceptions are worth learning with it: putrefy (to rot), rarefy (to make less dense) and stupefy (to astonish or daze).

 

NOTE

 

• Liquify (Option 2): By far the commonest misspelling, produced by treating the word as though it were built on *liquid*. It is the answer most candidates choose.

 

• Liqufy (Option 3): Drops a vowel altogether, giving a form that cannot be pronounced as the word is.

 

• Liquifye (Option 4): Adds a final e, which no English verb of this family takes.

question:
Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose the option "No replacement required".

The clerk’s inadvertant omission of one page delayed the whole file by a fortnight.
solution_text:
The correct answer is inadvertent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word in the sentence is spelt "inadvertant", which is incorrect. The correct spelling is INADVERTENT, meaning unintentional; done without attention or by oversight.

 

• The ending is -ENT, not *-ant*. The word is built from Latin in- ("not") + advertere ("to turn the mind to") — literally *not attending*.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The clerk's inadvertent omission of one page delayed the whole file by a fortnight.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The -ent / -ant split has no rule that covers every case, and both groups must be learnt:

 

• -ENT: inadvertent, independent, superintendent, persistent, competent, consistent, permanent, prominent, coherent

 

• -ANT: important, relevant, significant, defendant, assistant, applicant, tolerant, ignorant, abundant

 

• Note the adverb inadvertently, which is common in official English: *the file was inadvertently destroyed*.

 

NOTE

 

• inadvertunt (Option 1): An invented ending; -unt does not occur in English adjectives of this type.

 

• inadvertaint (Option 3): Another invented form, inserting an i before the ending.

 

• No replacement required (Option 4): This would be right only if the given word were already correct. Since the sentence reads "inadvertant", a replacement is required.

question:
There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.

The archaeologist described the find as an unpresidented discovery of considerable significance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is unpresidented.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The misspelt word is "unpresidented". The correct spelling is UNPRECEDENTED, meaning never having happened before; without any earlier example.

 

• The error is a confusion of two quite different words:

 

• PRECEDENT – an earlier instance that serves as an example or a rule. The word behind *unprecedented*.

 

• PRESIDENT – the head of a state or an organisation.

 

• The stem is pre-CEDE, from Latin *praecedere*, "to go before" — the same root as *precede*, *antecedent* and *recede*. There is no s in it.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The archaeologist described the find as an unprecedented discovery of considerable significance.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Note also the distinction between precedent (an earlier example) and precedence (priority in order or rank) — *the case set a precedent*, but *the Chief Justice takes precedence over the judges*.

 

NOTE

 

• archaeologist (Option 1): Correctly spelt. Note the -ae- after the initial *arch*, which the American spelling *archeologist* drops. The British form given here is the one SSC papers follow.

 

• significance (Option 2): Correctly spelt, with the ending -ance. It is placed here because the *-ance / -ence* choice is itself a common trap — but this word takes -ance.

 

• considerable (Option 3): Correctly spelt, with the ending -able, since the stem *consider* is a complete English word.

question: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Divisable.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The misspelt word is "Divisable". The correct spelling is DIVISIBLE, meaning capable of being divided.

 

• The ending is -IBLE, not *-able*, and there is a working rule that decides most cases:

 

• If the stem left after removing the ending is a complete English word, the ending is usually -ABLE — *depend + able*, *comfort + able*, *read + able*.

 

• If the stem is not a complete word, the ending is usually -IBLE — *divis-*, *permiss-*, *compat-*, *aud-*, *vis-*, *terr-*.

 

• *Divis-* is not an English word, so the ending must be -ible.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Common -IBLE words worth memorising: divisible, permissible, compatible, audible, visible, legible, tangible, feasible, plausible, eligible, negligible, susceptible, responsible, flexible, edible, horrible, terrible.

 

• The rule has exceptions in both directions — accessible and collapsible take *-ible* though the stems look complete, and inevitable takes *-able* though it does not — so the lists must still be learnt.

 

NOTE

 

• Permissible (Option 1): Correctly spelt. The stem *permiss-* is not a word, so -ible is right.

 

• Dependable (Option 2): Correctly spelt. The stem *depend* is a word, so -able is right.

 

• Compatible (Option 4): Correctly spelt, with -ible on the incomplete stem *compat-*.

question: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to "augment".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Diminish.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Augment (verb) means to make something greater by adding to it; to increase.

 

• Its direct antonym is Diminish, meaning to make or become less.

 

• Example: *He augmented his salary by teaching in the evenings, and diminished his expenses at the same time.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word comes from Latin augere, "to increase" — the same root that gives auction (a sale by increasing bids), author and augmentation.

 

• Note the special sense of augmented in music, where an augmented interval is one widened by a semitone.

 

• Other antonyms: reduce, curtail, abate, lessen, dwindle, contract.

 

NOTE

 

• The question is built so that three of the four options are synonyms of the key word and only one is its opposite. Recognising that shape at once is faster than weighing each option separately.

 

• Increase (Option 1): The plainest synonym of augment.

 

• Enlarge (Option 2): Means to make bigger in size — a second synonym, differing only in applying chiefly to physical extent.

 

• Amplify (Option 4): Means to increase in strength or in detail — a third synonym, used of sound and of statements alike.

question: Choose the word that is the antonym of "innate".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Acquired.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Innate (adjective) means inborn; present in a person from birth rather than learnt.

 

• Its direct antonym is Acquired, meaning gained or developed later, through learning or experience.

 

• Example: *His sense of rhythm seemed innate; his command of the language was plainly acquired.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The pair innate / acquired underlies a long argument in psychology, usually put as "nature versus nurture" — how much of what a person is comes with him, and how much is added by his upbringing.

 

• The word comes from Latin innatus, "born in". Other antonyms: learnt, cultivated, developed, extrinsic.

 

NOTE

 

• Inborn (Option 1): Means possessed from birth — the plainest synonym of innate.

 

• Inherent (Option 2): Means existing in something as a permanent and essential attribute — a second synonym, though it applies to things as well as to persons.

 

• Congenital (Option 4): Means present from birth, and is used chiefly of medical conditions (*a congenital defect*). A third synonym, and the hardest of the four words.

question:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The two reports were not rivals; each was a _____ to the other, supplying what the other lacked.
solution_text:
The correct answer is complement.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct word is complement, a noun meaning something that completes another, or that supplies what it lacks.

 

• Completed sentence: *The two reports were not rivals; each was a complement to the other, supplying what the other lacked.*

 

• The clue is in the sentence itself — *"supplying what the other lacked"* is a definition of a complement.

 

• The whole difficulty of the question lies in a pair of words that sound identical:

 

• COMPLEMENT (with an e) – to complete. Remember: com-plE-ment completes.

 

• COMPLIMENT (with an i) – to praise. Remember: com-plI-ment is what I give you.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Both words also work as verbs: *the wine complements the dish* (completes it); *he complimented her on the speech* (praised her).

 

• The word complement has technical senses too — in grammar, the word or phrase completing the predicate; in mathematics, the angle that completes a right angle.

 

NOTE

 

• compliment (Option 2): Means an expression of praise. The sentence describes two reports completing each other, not praising each other.

 

• complementary (Option 3): The adjective from *complement*. The blank follows the article "a" and requires a noun, so an adjective cannot stand there.

 

• complimentary (Option 4): The adjective from *compliment*, meaning praising — or, in a second sense, given free of charge (*a complimentary ticket*). Wrong on both counts here: wrong word, and wrong part of speech.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

The art or practice of drawing maps and charts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cartography.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Cartography is the art and science of making maps and charts.

 

• The word is formed from French carte ("map") + Greek graphein ("to write or draw").

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The -graphy family is examined constantly, and the whole set is worth learning together:

 

• Cartography – map-making; Topography – the description of the surface features of a place

 

• Calligraphy – beautiful handwriting; Typography – the design and arrangement of printed type

 

• Choreography – the composition of dance; Cinematography – motion-picture photography

 

• Lithography – printing from a flat stone or metal plate

 

• Lexicography – the compiling of dictionaries; Bibliography – a list of books

 

• Geography – the study of the earth; Oceanography – the study of the sea

 

NOTE

 

• Choreography (Option 2): The arrangement of the steps and movements of a dance, from Greek *khoreia*, "dance".

 

• Lithography (Option 3): A method of printing from a stone or metal surface, from *lithos*, "stone". It is a printing process, not a form of drawing maps.

 

• Topography (Option 4): The closest distractor. Topography is the detailed description of the physical features of a place — the hills, rivers and valleys themselves — whereas cartography is the making of the map on which they are shown.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

The art of preparing and mounting the skins of dead animals so that they appear lifelike.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Taxidermy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Taxidermy is the art of preparing, stuffing and mounting the skins of animals so that they have a lifelike appearance, as for a museum or a collection.

 

• The word is formed from Greek taxis ("arrangement") + derma ("skin") — literally *the arranging of skin*. One who practises it is a taxidermist.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• A group of taxis-words worth holding together: taxidermy (arranging skin), taxonomy (arranging names, that is, classification), syntax (the arranging of words in a sentence).

 

• A group of derma-words: dermatology (the study of the skin), epidermis (the outer layer of skin), hypodermic (under the skin), pachyderm (a thick-skinned animal, such as the elephant).

 

NOTE

 

• Taxonomy (Option 1): The science of classification, especially of living organisms into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. It shares the *taxis* element, which is exactly what makes it the closest distractor.

 

• Embalming (Option 2): The preservation of a dead body from decay, by treating it with spices or chemicals. It applies to the whole body, usually human, and its purpose is preservation rather than lifelike display.

 

• Anatomy (Option 3): The study of the structure of the body, learnt chiefly by dissection. It concerns what is inside, and it is a science rather than an art of presentation.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition or prepositional phrase in the following sentence.

_____ his repeated warnings, the villagers went on drawing water from the abandoned well.
solution_text:
The correct answer is In spite of.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence requires a phrase expressing concession — the villagers went on doing something although they had been warned against it.

 

• The only phrase of concession among the four is in spite of, meaning *despite; notwithstanding*.

 

• Completed sentence: *In spite of his repeated warnings, the villagers went on drawing water from the abandoned well.*

 

• The other three all express cause, and any of them would reverse the sense — making the warnings the reason for drawing the water rather than a reason against it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Prepositional phrases grouped by the relation they express — the whole of this question type lies in knowing which group a phrase belongs to:

 

• Concession: in spite of, despite, notwithstanding, regardless of, for all

 

• Cause: because of, owing to, due to, on account of, in view of, as a result of

 

• Substitution: in lieu of, in place of, instead of

 

• Reference: with regard to, in respect of, with reference to

 

• Note that despite takes no "of" — *despite the warnings*, never *despite of the warnings*.

 

NOTE

 

• Because of (Option 2): Expresses cause. It would mean the warnings caused the villagers to draw the water, which is absurd.

 

• In view of (Option 3): Expresses cause or consideration — *in view of the shortage, rationing was imposed*. Again the sense would be reversed.

 

• On account of (Option 4): A third phrase of cause, and interchangeable with *because of*. Three cause phrases are offered against one of concession, which is the design of the question.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into the passive voice?

The bank charges a penalty for every late instalment.
option_1: A penalty was charged by the bank for every late instalment.
option_2: A penalty is being charged by the bank for every late instalment.
option_3: A penalty is charged by the bank for every late instalment.
option_4: A penalty has been charged by the bank for every late instalment.
solution_text:
The correct answer is A penalty is charged by the bank for every late instalment.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Simple Present tense, active voice: *"The bank charges a penalty."*

 

• The rule for converting the Simple Present into the passive is:

 

• is / am / are + past participle (V3)

 

• Here the new subject, "a penalty", is singular, so the auxiliary is is, and the past participle of *charge* is charged.

 

• The steps of conversion are the same in every case:

 

• The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive

 

• The verb takes the passive form belonging to that tense

 

• The subject of the active sentence becomes the agent, introduced by by

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Passive forms of the tenses — the table to memorise:

 

• Simple Present – is/am/are + V3

 

• Present Continuous – is/am/are being + V3

 

• Present Perfect – has/have been + V3

 

• Simple Past – was/were + V3

 

• Past Continuous – was/were being + V3

 

• Past Perfect – had been + V3

 

• Simple Future – will be + V3; Future Perfect – will have been + V3

 

• Modals – modal + be + V3

 

• Note that the Perfect Continuous tenses and the Future Continuous have no passive form in ordinary use.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 uses was charged, the passive of the Simple Past. The original is in the present tense, and the tense must never be altered in conversion.

 

• Option 2 uses is being charged, the passive of the Present Continuous, which would mean the charge is being levied at this moment. The sentence describes a standing practice.

 

• Option 4 uses has been charged, the passive of the Present Perfect, which reports a completed action — again a change of tense.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into the passive voice?

Where did the postman deliver the parcel yesterday?
option_1: Where is the parcel delivered by the postman yesterday?
option_2: Where did the parcel delivered by the postman yesterday?
option_3: Where were the parcel delivered by the postman yesterday?
option_4: Where was the parcel delivered by the postman yesterday?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Where was the parcel delivered by the postman yesterday?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Two things must be handled together here: the sentence is interrogative, and it is in the Simple Past tense.

 

• The tense. *"Where did the postman deliver..."* is the Simple Past. Its passive is was / were + V3. Note that the tense is carried by *did*, which is why the main verb appears in its base form in the active question — and why the participle required in the passive is delivered.

 

• The number. The new subject is "the parcel", which is singular, so the auxiliary must be was, not *were*.

 

• The word order. In a question beginning with an interrogative word such as *where*, *when* or *why*, the passive keeps that word first and the auxiliary follows it:

 

• Where + was/were + subject + V3 + by + agent?

 

• The adverb "yesterday" confirms the Simple Past and rules out any present form.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Interrogative sentences in the passive — the three patterns:

 

• With do / does / did: *Did he post the letter?* → Was the letter posted by him?

 

• With who: *Who wrote this note?* → By whom was this note written?

 

• With what / when / where / why / how: the question word stays in front, and the auxiliary follows it.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 uses is delivered, the passive of the Simple Present, which cannot stand with *yesterday*.

 

• Option 2 keeps the auxiliary did and adds the participle *delivered*, producing a construction that does not exist in English. Once *did* is present the verb must be in its base form, and *did* has no place in a passive sentence at all.

 

• Option 3 uses were, which does not agree with the singular subject *the parcel*.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into the active voice?

A new procedure for the disposal of waste has been recommended by the expert committee.
option_1: The expert committee recommended a new procedure for the disposal of waste.
option_2: The expert committee is recommending a new procedure for the disposal of waste.
option_3: The expert committee has recommended a new procedure for the disposal of waste.
option_4: The expert committee had recommended a new procedure for the disposal of waste.
solution_text:
The correct answer is The expert committee has recommended a new procedure for the disposal of waste.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Present Perfect, passive voice: *"...has been recommended by the expert committee."*

 

• The passive form has / have been + V3 corresponds to the active form has / have + V3.

 

• In converting to the active voice:

 

• The agent — *the expert committee* — becomes the subject

 

• The subject of the passive — *a new procedure* — becomes the object

 

• The verb becomes has recommended, the auxiliary agreeing with the singular subject *committee*

 

• The word by disappears, since there is no longer an agent to introduce.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Conversion from passive to active is simply the reverse of the ordinary process, and the tense is the thing most often lost in it. A reliable method is to identify the passive form first, and then write down the active form that corresponds to it:

 

• *is/am/are + V3* → V1 / V5

 

• *was/were + V3* → V2

 

• *has/have been + V3* → has/have + V3

 

• *had been + V3* → had + V3

 

• *will be + V3* → will + V1

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 uses recommended, the Simple Past. The passive sentence is in the Present Perfect, and the two are not interchangeable — the Present Perfect connects the action to the present, the Simple Past does not.

 

• Option 2 uses is recommending, the Present Continuous, which would mean the recommendation is being made at this moment.

 

• Option 4 uses had recommended, the Past Perfect, which corresponds to the passive *had been recommended*, not to *has been recommended*.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into the active voice?

No objection was raised by any member of the committee.
option_1: No member of the committee raised any objection.
option_2: Any member of the committee did not raise an objection.
option_3: No member of the committee has raised any objection.
option_4: Not any member of the committee raised an objection.
solution_text:
The correct answer is No member of the committee raised any objection.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is negative and in the passive voice, Simple Past: *"No objection was raised by any member."*

 

• Converting a negative sentence needs care, because the words no and any exchange places:

 

• In the passive, the negative attaches to the object — *no objection*

 

• In the active, it must attach to the subject — *no member*

 

• The remaining *any* moves to the object: *any objection*

 

• The tense. The passive was + V3 corresponds to the active V2, so *was raised* becomes raised.

 

• The agent *by any member of the committee* becomes the subject, and by disappears.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The rule of English worth remembering here is that "no" belongs at the head of the clause. English prefers *No member came* to *Any member did not come*; the second is understood, but it is not idiomatic, and in an examination it is marked wrong.

 

• The same principle governs never, nobody and nothing: *Nothing was said by him* → He said nothing, not *He did not say anything* — though the latter is acceptable English, it is not the direct conversion.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 places any in the subject and the negative in the verb — *"Any member... did not raise"*. This is precisely the construction English avoids.

 

• Option 3 uses has raised, the Present Perfect. The passive sentence is in the Simple Past, and the tense must be preserved.

 

• Option 4 uses "Not any member", which is grammatically possible but never idiomatic. Where English has a single word — no — it does not use two.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

He was implicated _____ the conspiracy on the testimony of a single witness.
solution_text:
The correct answer is in.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb implicate is followed by the preposition in: *to be implicated in a crime, in a conspiracy, in a scandal*.

 

• Completed sentence: *He was implicated in the conspiracy on the testimony of a single witness.*

 

• To implicate means to show or suggest that somebody is involved in something wrong.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Verbs of involvement and participation take in: *implicated in, involved in, engaged in, absorbed in, engrossed in, participate in, indulge in, succeed in, persist in*.

 

• Note the related noun implication, which has two distinct senses: involvement in wrongdoing, and something suggested but not stated.

 

• Distinguish implicate from imply: to *imply* is to suggest something without saying it; to *implicate* is to involve someone in a charge.

 

NOTE

 

• with (Option 1): The strongest distractor, because *charged with*, *accused of* and *connected with* are all common in the same context. But *implicate* keeps its own preposition.

 

• for (Option 2): Used with *tried for, punished for, arrested for, prosecuted for* — verbs concerning the offence rather than the involvement.

 

• to (Option 3): Used with *party to a conspiracy* — a phrase very close in meaning, which is why it is placed here. One is a party to a conspiracy but implicated in it.

question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the alternative that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case the first three alternatives are not found suitable, choose the last one, "No improvement required".

The witness gave an account so incredulous that the court refused to act on it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is so incredible that the court.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is a confusion of two words that look alike and mean quite different things:

 

• INCREDIBLE – unbelievable; describes a thing, a statement or an account

 

• INCREDULOUS – unwilling or unable to believe; describes a person and his state of mind

 

• Here the word qualifies "an account", which is a thing. An account can be *incredible*; only a person can be *incredulous*.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The witness gave an account so incredible that the court refused to act on it.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other pairs distinguished in exactly the same way — the first describing the thing, the second the person:

 

• incredible / incredulous – unbelievable / disbelieving

 

• contemptible / contemptuous – deserving scorn / showing scorn

 

• pitiable / pitiful and pitying – deserving pity / feeling pity

 

• respectable / respectful – deserving respect / showing respect

 

• enviable / envious – to be envied / feeling envy

 

• credible / credulous – believable / too ready to believe

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 repeats the underlined phrase unchanged, and so improves nothing.

 

• Option 3 offers credulous, which means too ready to believe. It is the opposite of what is meant, and applies to a person in any case.

 

• Option 4 cannot be right, since the sentence as it stands attributes a state of mind to a document.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The Deputy Commissioner ordered a survey of every well in the district.
A. The forms were printed in July and sent out to the tehsils in August.
B. Of the eleven hundred wells listed in the final return, four hundred were found to have been filled in years earlier.
C. The survey was reported complete in November, three months behind the date that had been fixed for it.
D. Each form carried thirty-one columns, of which nineteen concerned the depth of the water at different seasons.
S2. The file was marked "for further study" and placed in the record room, where it has remained.
solution_text:
The correct answer is ADCB.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The paragraph is governed by a calendar — July, August, November — and by the natural order in which an administrative exercise proceeds.

 

• A must open the sequence. It carries the earliest dates, July and August, and it introduces the forms, which the next sentence describes.

 

• D follows A directly. *"Each form carried thirty-one columns"* takes up the forms of A; a description of the form can only come after the form has been mentioned.

 

• C follows D, carrying the later date — November — and reporting the completion of the survey.

 

• B must be last of the four. It speaks of the "final return", which exists only once the survey has been reported complete in C, and it delivers the finding towards which the whole paragraph has been moving.

 

• S2 then closes on the file being marked for further study and put away — the flat administrative ending that gives the paragraph its point.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The paragraph has the shape order → preparation → description → completion → finding → nothing done. Where a paragraph ends with an anticlimax of this kind, the substantial finding almost always stands immediately before it, so that the contrast is felt.

 

NOTE

 

• BADC (Option 2): Opens with B, so the final return is described before a single form has been printed.

 

• DCBA (Option 3): Opens with D, whose *"Each form"* refers to forms not yet introduced.

 

• CBAD (Option 4): Opens with C, so the survey is completed in November before it has begun in July, and the dates run backwards.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Ranjan’s grandmother had never in her life travelled further than the next district.
A. She agreed at last, on the single condition that she be allowed to carry her own bedding.
B. When he was posted to Bombay he wrote asking her to come and stay with him for a month.
C. She looked at it for a long while and then asked him whether the sea was always that colour.
D. On the second evening he took her down to the shore and showed her the sea.
S2. He said that it was not, and she nodded as though he had confirmed something she had suspected for years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is BADC.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• B must open the sequence. S1 tells us only that the grandmother had never travelled; B supplies the invitation that sets everything else in motion. Every other sentence presupposes that she has been asked.

 

• A follows B. *"She agreed at last"* is a response to an invitation, and the invitation is in B. The phrase *"at last"* also implies a period of persuasion, which belongs immediately after the asking.

 

• D follows A. The journey has been agreed to, so she has arrived, and *"on the second evening"* places us in Bombay. D introduces the sea.

 

• C must be last of the four. *"She looked at it"* refers to the sea of D, and the question she asks is what S2 answers.

 

• S2 — *"He said that it was not"* — replies directly to the question in C, which confirms that C stands immediately before it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Two links settle this question, and both are worth carrying into the examination hall:

 

• A pronoun (*it* in C) must follow the noun it stands for (*the sea* in D).

 

• A reply (S2) must follow the question it answers (C).

 

NOTE

 

• CDBA (Option 1): Opens with C, so she looks at something that has not been mentioned, and asks a question that S2 answers four sentences later.

 

• ADBC (Option 2): Opens with A, so she agrees to an invitation that has not yet been made.

 

• ADCB (Option 4): Wrong on the same count at the opening, and it also places C before B, separating the question from the answer in S2.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The clock on the courthouse tower had shown twenty past four for as long as the town could remember.
A. A committee was appointed, subscriptions were raised, and a mechanic was sent for from Nagpur.
B. In the year of the centenary somebody proposed that it should be put right.
C. He examined it for two days and reported that there was nothing whatever wrong with the mechanism.
D. Somebody, at some time, had simply stopped it, and nobody had afterwards thought to start it again.
S2. The committee considered his report, thanked him for his trouble, and did not meet again.
solution_text:
The correct answer is BACD.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• B must open the sequence. S1 describes a state of affairs that has lasted for generations; B supplies the occasion on which something was at last proposed — the year of the centenary. Nothing else can precede it, because every other sentence follows from the proposal.

 

• A follows B. The committee, the subscriptions and the summoning of the mechanic are all consequences of the proposal, and A introduces the mechanic.

 

• C follows A. The pronoun "He" can only be the mechanic of A, and C gives his examination and his report.

 

• D must be last of the four. It is the content of the report — the explanation of why nothing was wrong — and it delivers the point the whole paragraph has been building towards.

 

• S2 then closes on the committee thanking him and never meeting again, which is intelligible only once we know how little there was to be done.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The paragraph works by deflation: an elaborate machinery of committees and subscriptions is set up to solve a problem that turns out to require nothing but the winding of a key. The order matters because the deflation must come last — a joke told out of order is not a joke.

 

NOTE

 

• ADCB (Option 1): Opens with A, so a committee is appointed before anybody has proposed anything.

 

• ACBD (Option 2): Opens with A on the same wrong footing, and places B after C, so the proposal comes after the mechanic has already submitted his report.

 

• CBAD (Option 4): Opens with C, whose *"He"* has no antecedent, since the mechanic is introduced only in A.

question:
The following sentence is divided into four parts, given in the alternatives 1, 2, 3 and 4. Select the alternative which contains the part of the sentence that has an error.

The principal called for/ an unanimous decision/ from all the members/ of the governing body.
solution_text:
The correct answer is an unanimous decision.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is in the article. It should be "a unanimous decision", not *an unanimous*.

 

• The rule governing a and an depends on sound, not on spelling:

 

• A is used before a word beginning with a consonant SOUND

 

• AN is used before a word beginning with a vowel SOUND

 

• Although unanimous begins with the letter u, it is pronounced "yoo-nan-i-mous" — beginning with the consonant sound /j/, as in *yes*. It therefore takes a.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The principal called for a unanimous decision from all the members of the governing body.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Words beginning with a vowel letter but a consonant sound — all take "a":

 

• a unanimous decision, a university, a union, a useful book, a uniform, a European, a one-rupee note, a one-way street

 

• Words beginning with a consonant letter but a vowel sound — all take "an":

 

• an hour, an honest man, an honour, an heir, an MP, an MLA, an SDM, an X-ray, an LLB degree

 

• The test is always to say the word aloud and listen to the first sound.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is correct. *"Called for"* is the right phrasal verb, meaning *demanded* or *required*.

 

• Option 3 is correct. *"From all the members"* uses the right preposition, since the decision is sought from them.

 

• Option 4 is correct. *"Of the governing body"* properly qualifies *the members*.

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:

 

Protein is often called the building material of the body, and the description is an exact one. Every cell contains it, and the tissues that must be renewed most often — the skin, the hair, the nails and the lining of the gut — are built almost entirely from it. Proteins are made of smaller units called amino acids, of which twenty are used by the human body. Eleven of these the body can manufacture for itself; the remaining nine it cannot, and these are called essential amino acids because they _____ obtained from food. A food that supplies all nine in sufficient quantity is called a complete protein, and milk, eggs, fish and soya are of this kind. Most plant foods are incomplete, lacking one or another of the nine — but what is missing from one is often present in another, which is why the old combination of a cereal with a pulse, of rice with dal or of roti with chana, supplies between them what neither supplies alone. Growing children, expectant mothers and those recovering from illness need more protein than others, and a prolonged shortage of it in early childhood produces the wasting condition known as kwashiorkor. Eat a variety of foods rather than a great deal of any one. It is the simplest rule in nutrition, and the most often ignored.

 

Choose the option that correctly fills the blank in the passage: "...these are called essential amino acids because they _____ obtained from food."
solution_text:
The correct answer is must be.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank requires a modal verb in the passive voice, and the rule is fixed: modal + BE + past participle (V3).

 

• Here the modal is must, and the participle is obtained, so the form is must be obtained.

 

• The sense confirms it. The passage says the body cannot manufacture these nine amino acids, so obtaining them from food is a necessity — and *must* is the modal of necessity.

 

• The completed sentence reads: *...these are called essential amino acids because they must be obtained from food.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Modals in the passive follow one pattern without exception:

 

• *The work must be done.* • *It can be repaired.*

 

• *This should be avoided.* • *It may be postponed.*

 

• For the perfect passive, the form is modal + have been + V3: *It must have been lost.*

 

NOTE

 

• must have (Option 2): Would give *"must have obtained"*, which is active and would mean the amino acids did the obtaining — a reversal of the sense.

 

• were being (Option 3): The past continuous passive. The passage states a permanent scientific fact, which takes the present tense, not a past one.

 

• has been (Option 4): The present perfect passive, and singular besides. The subject "they" is plural and would require *have been*, and a perfect tense would report a completed event rather than a standing necessity.

The sentence "Eat a variety of foods rather than a great deal of any one." is an example of which type of sentence?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Imperative.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence "Eat a variety of foods rather than a great deal of any one." is IMPERATIVE, because it gives a command, an instruction or a piece of advice.

 

• Two marks identify an imperative sentence, and both are present here:

 

• The verb is in its base form — *Eat*

 

• The subject is not stated. It is understood to be "you", which is why an imperative can begin directly with the verb.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four types of sentence by function:

 

• Declarative (assertive) – makes a statement; ends with a full stop. *Protein is the building material of the body.*

 

• Interrogative – asks a question; ends with a question mark. *What are amino acids?*

 

• Imperative – gives a command, request or advice; the subject *you* is understood. *Eat a variety of foods.*

 

• Exclamatory – expresses sudden or strong feeling; ends with an exclamation mark. *How simple the rule is!*

 

• A request is imperative just as a command is — *Please pass the salt* is imperative, though it orders nobody.

 

NOTE

 

• Declarative (Option 1): Would require the sentence to state a fact. Most of the passage is declarative, but this sentence does not state anything — it directs.

 

• Interrogative (Option 2): Would require a question, and there is no question mark and no inversion of subject and verb.

 

• Exclamatory (Option 4): Would require an expression of strong feeling and, ordinarily, an exclamation mark. The sentence is calm advice.

Which word is the closest in meaning to "sufficient" as it is used in the passage?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Adequate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the passage, "sufficient" appears in the phrase *"a food that supplies all nine in sufficient quantity"* — that is, in a quantity that is enough for the purpose.

 

• Its closest synonym is Adequate, which likewise means *enough; as much as is required*.

 

• Note that both words mean enough and no more. Neither implies a surplus, and that is the distinction the question turns on.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other synonyms: ample, enough, satisfactory, commensurate.

 

• The noun is sufficiency, and the negative insufficient. The phrase "self-sufficient" means able to supply one's own needs without help — a term of constant use in economics.

 

NOTE

 

• Scarce (Option 1): Means insufficient; hard to obtain — the direct antonym of sufficient.

 

• Excessive (Option 3): Means more than is necessary. This is the subtlest distractor of the three: a quantity may be excessive and still, obviously, be sufficient — but the two words are not synonyms, because *sufficient* says nothing about surplus.

 

• Doubtful (Option 4): Means uncertain. It concerns confidence, not quantity, and has no bearing on the sense of the word in the passage.

According to the passage, why does the traditional combination of a cereal with a pulse work well?
option_1: Because cereals and pulses are the cheapest of all foods available
option_2: Because what is missing from one is present in the other, so that between them they supply all nine essential amino acids
option_3: Because pulses contain all nine essential amino acids on their own
option_4: Because cereals prevent the body from losing the protein it already has
solution_text:
The correct answer is Because what is missing from one is present in the other, so that between them they supply all nine essential amino acids.

• The passage states the reason directly: *"Most plant foods are incomplete, lacking one or another of the nine — but what is missing from one is often present in another, which is why the old combination of a cereal with a pulse... supplies between them what neither supplies alone."*

 

• The principle is one of mutual completion. Neither food is a complete protein by itself; taken together, the gaps in each are filled by the other.

 

• The examples the passage gives are rice with dal and roti with chana.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

• Nutritionists call this protein complementation, and it is the reason a vegetarian diet can supply complete protein without any animal food at all — provided the combination is right.

 

• The traditional cuisines of many countries arrived at the same solution independently: rice and dal in India, corn and beans in Mexico, rice and soya in East Asia.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 offers cost as the explanation. The passage nowhere mentions the price of any food.

 

• Option 3 claims pulses are complete proteins by themselves. The passage says the opposite — *"most plant foods are incomplete"* — and the complete proteins it names are milk, eggs, fish and soya.
